1:
The adversative that opens the chapter is felt by everyone. Gill takes it as marking dependence on what has just been said, so that though the hill the temple stood on should be made desolate, the thing it typified should be exalted and enlarged. Henry works the contrast into an image, the mountain left as waste as the high places of the forest and now as much dignified by being frequented as ever it was disgraced by being deserted, and says that out of the ashes of the church another phoenix shall arise. Ellicott calls it a sudden transition, a vision of light rising upon a chapter closed in deepest gloom. Keil and Delitzsch state it as the governing thought, Zion exalted from the deepest degradation to the highest glory, and set out the structure that follows: first the glorifying of the mountain by the streaming of the nations to it, then the restoration of Zion's dominion and its conflict with the nations of the world. Calvin locates the change in the audience. Having spoken to the whole people and their rulers, the prophet now turns aside to the faithful few, since others were not capable of receiving the consolation; and Calvin makes it a rule about teaching, that threatenings must be moderated when the children of God are in view, since the more a man is touched with the fear of God the more he dreads his judgment and is fearful enough already.

Who wrote these verses first is the one properly contested question. Clarke reports a judgment that this prophet took the passage from the other, and offers two alternatives, that the Spirit inspired both with the same prediction, or that both copied a common original well known at the time. Ellicott calls it almost an open question, quotes a decided modern claim that the prophecy was originally delivered here and that no one now thinks it adopted from the other prophet, and declines to accept it: the statement is far too sweeping, and all that can correctly be said is that the preponderance of opinion favours this prophet. Henry sets the question aside by making the coincidence the point, that two prophets said the very same thing at the same time so that the promises might be established out of the mouth of two witnesses.

When the last days are is answered on two levels, and one voice keeps both. Gill takes them for the days of the Messiah, following a Jewish commentator, and subdivides: the first of those days were the days of Christ in the flesh with his forerunner and his disciples, which were also the last days of the Jewish state, while what is promised here belongs to the last of them. Clarke likewise refers the fulfilment to the coming of the Messiah and the apostles preaching from Jerusalem outwards, and cautions that the closing verses have been applied to the conquests of the Maccabees, though those exploits correspond only in a very faint degree to the highly wrought terms of the prophecy. Henry finds the same reading conceded by some of the rabbins and describes what is promised as a new charter, with a new way of worship and a new institution of offices. Wesley alone gives the words a nearer historical anchor before the further one: the latter days are the expiring of the seventy years of captivity, nearly two hundred years from the prophet's own time, and the establishing was literally fulfilled when the second temple was built and only spiritually fulfilled when the church was founded by the preaching of the gospel. Ellicott takes the elevation figuratively throughout, the mountain spiritually raised above all else, visible and invisible, and established for ever; and Calvin draws the widest inference, that the calling of the Gentiles, and so the salvation of his own readers, is contained in this prophecy.
2:
The word many is where Calvin puts the weight. Gill notes only that the parallel passage has a different word for the peoples and that the sense is the same. Calvin makes the difference substantial: it was already said nations would come, and the addition says more, since the earlier king had made some nations tributary but his borders were narrow compared with what is promised. He then draws the conclusion the comparison is for: this kingdom is spiritual. Tribute could be imposed on the conquered, but they were never brought to the pure worship of God nor united in one faith; here the nations speak for themselves and come voluntarily. Ellicott reads the verse as preparing for more definite prophecies, a common consent among the nations journeying forth, asking the way in this world and finding the house in the eternal one; and to this day, he observes, the hearts of Jews and Christians alike yearn towards Jerusalem. Wesley finds partial fulfilments already: proselyted servants who came up with their masters, and the released captives encouraging one another, with the conversion of the Gentiles as the more eminent fulfilment. Keil and Delitzsch add a caution, that the race will reach this goal not through general humanitarian ideas and efforts but solely through the omnipotence and faithfulness of the Lord.

The going forth of the law is for Calvin the reason for all promised before it, and he presses two details. The fulfilment was literal at the beginning of the gospel, first preached at Jerusalem, so that what is predicted was in part accomplished then and will be more completely accomplished hereafter. And the phrase is on the top of the mountains, not of a mountain, from which he infers that the church was never to be confined to one place but pre-eminent throughout the earth, coextensive with the word that went out. He returns to the manner of the submission: people are not constrained by armed force or the sword, but really reformed, so that they yield a voluntary service and renounce their own superstitions. Wesley keeps the clause local: in Jerusalem the only way of worshipping God is declared, and from there the only law of right worship goes out.

Who does the judging in the next verse is disputed. Gill reports that three Jewish commentators make it the King Messiah, and that some render the verb impersonally, interpreting it of the church, or of the word and doctrine, or of the Lord acting by the ministry of the word. Calvin knows the same division, whether the subject is the Lord himself or his word, and states his own view flatly, that it is certainly God who is spoken of, the verb meaning to rule, so that nations which had not obeyed him now own him as king. He then makes the distinction that governs his reading: God governs the devil and the wicked too, but not by his word nor by the sanctifying power of his Spirit, so that they obey against their will, whereas his peculiar government is of his church only, where by word and Spirit he bends hearts to follow willingly. Gill adds a note on the words afar off, absent from the parallel passage, and reports the Targum taking them of time rather than distance, so the kingdom reaches both to the ends of the earth and to distant ages. Ellicott lets the promise stand against the present: the name of the Messiah is the Prince of Peace, and we look for the full realisation of his reign out of a life still rife with wars, sure the time will come because the mouth of the Lord has spoken it. Calvin describes the same effect as the fruit of divine truth, men who burned with the lust of doing harm having their disposition changed and devoting themselves to acts of kindness.
4:
The vine and the fig tree are agreed to be proverbial and are then pressed in different directions. Gill and Clarke both call the phrase proverbial of tranquillity, Gill adding that men need not keep within walled towns and lock themselves in their houses but may sit down in their gardens and fields and enjoy the fruit. Clarke adds a textual observation the others do not, that this verse is an addition to the prophecy as it stands in the parallel passage. Ellicott gives the proverb a historical reference, the security of a peace no foreign power was strong enough to disturb, and identifies it with the state of the nation under Solomon, when Judah and Israel dwelt safely from one end of the land to the other. Wesley makes it the peace of the redeemed from captivity, a type of a greater redemption. Calvin asks why these trees are named rather than the dwelling-house, and answers that the point is exposure: it might have been said that a man lives securely at home, but here he is in the open and fears no violence, because those who were thieves will observe what is just and those who were bloody will study to do good, so that a man may leave his door unclosed, sleep in the open air and still be safe. He takes the verse to include two things, that hostilities cease, and that real happiness cannot exist unless Christ rules men by his gospel, since without it every man fears for himself, and peace is the chief good.

The next verse is felt as a difficulty, though only one voice states it as one. Gill takes it of the interval: until the promised times come the nations retain their former religion, either until otherwise instructed or, as another commentator has it, until the Messiah turns them into the right way; and he brings the observation down to his own day with a list of those still walking in the name of their own gods. Clarke reads the contrast the other way, that this is the state of the Gentile world, whereas after the captivity the Jews walked in the name of the Lord alone and have acknowledged no other object of worship since. Wesley reduces the clause to a fact of custom, that it is the practice of all nations to serve their gods. Ellicott explains the sequence by the way prophecy works: the near future and the distant one are blended in the vision, as in the prophecies of our Lord the destruction of the city is described in terms finally accomplished in the day of judgment; the rule described here applies primarily to the prosperity following the return, whose zeal he thinks was stirred by having watched the devotion of the Babylonian princes to their own gods.

Calvin alone puts the objection sharply and answers it. There seems, he says, to be an inconsistency: it was just said that all nations would come and call one another to go up, and now that every people will walk in the name of its own god. His solution is that the verse does not describe the promised age but supports the faithful until it arrives. Israel driven into exile, their inheritance taken, the temple demolished and no visible religion left, might have been overwhelmed with despair, and the earlier promise needed such a confirmation; so the sense is that though the nations be divided into sects and each addicted to its own superstitions, these will continue firm in the pure worship of God and in unity of faith. He adds that such constancy is itself a fruit of the kingdom, since until Christ shines among us and rules by his word there is in us no firmness, whereas joined together under him nothing can turn us from the right course though the whole world were shaken.
6:
What the halting means divides the voices squarely. Clarke takes it of divided allegiance, that they halted between the true God and idols, and reads the other epithets to match, driven into captivity for that idolatry and afflicted because they would not return. Gill names that reading and rejects it, since it will not suit their present state, offering instead that they were like lame and maimed sheep, or that halting stands for sin, the word describing those who go sideways rather than uprightly. Calvin rejects it more bluntly: the root means the side, so those who walk only on one side are called halters, and the sense is maimed or weak; the reference to halting between two opinions he calls foreign to the drift of the passage. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, the feminine forms being neuter and collective, and take the limping for the miserable condition of the dispersed. Wesley makes it weakness under the hard usage of oppressing conquerors. On the remnant, Gill and Wesley both stress preservation for a seed, and Clarke adds that they were kept a distinct people after the return; he also quotes the Chaldee paraphrase, remarkable here because it applies the words positively to the Messiah as one hidden because of the congregation's sins.

The tower of the flock produces the widest disagreement in the chapter. Gill lays out four candidates without settling: a place of that name near Bethlehem, supposed to be where the shepherds watched when the birth was announced; Bethlehem itself; the sheep gate of Jerusalem and its tower, through which the entry is supposed to have been made; or the city itself. Clarke thinks the temple or Jerusalem is meant, where the whole congregation assembled to worship, and believes it is Jerusalem, or the temple, or both, these being the stronghold of the people. Ellicott argues from the figure, that the people having been compared to a flock, their city is called its tower or protection, and says outright that this is more satisfactory than the reading which makes it the place near Bethlehem. Calvin reports a reading he does not adopt, that the devastation of the city is meant, since it had become like a cottage, the second word being rendered obscure from a root meaning to cover; his own preference is that the holy city is so called because God chose it to gather his people, confirmed for him by the two clauses standing in apposition, the second explaining the first. He adds that if the other sense be preferred he will not contend. Wesley takes both terms as parts standing for the whole. Henry canvasses the same options and settles for the city, all the flock of Israel resorting there three times a year.

The first dominion is read as an unfulfilled promise by all who press it. Clarke identifies it with the divine theocracy under Christ, a former dominion to be restored, and finds confirmation in the name Immanuel, God ruling among us. Wesley distinguishes type from antitype, the government returning after the captivity to the former royal family until Shiloh come, fulfilled in the type under the returned governor while the whole antitype concerns the Messiah's kingdom. Henry makes the argument negatively: the promise is of a dignity equal to what the city had under its first two kings, and this by no means had its accomplishment under the governor of the return, whose rule was nothing like it either in splendour at home or extent of power abroad, so that it must refer to the Messiah's kingdom, as the Chaldee paraphrase also refers it. Keil and Delitzsch place the verse structurally, the prophecy turning from the glorifying of Zion to the throne founded by David and swept away with the city's destruction, and predicting its restoration, so that the promised reign is effected through a Davidic dominion.
9:
The two questions put to the mourning city are answered in flatly opposite tones. Clarke takes them as accusation and supplies the answers himself: is there no king? none, and the reason is that they had rejected the Lord their king; is the counsellor perished? no, but they had rejected the words and advices of the prophets. Wesley takes them as consolation and supplies the opposite answers: the earthly king is lost, but their God, their king, is with them; and though no wise counsellor may be left, the Wonderful Counsellor has the conduct of their sufferings, their deliverance and their re-establishment. Gill neither accuses nor consoles but attends to the cry itself, an emphatic doubled expression for a vehement lamentation raised as though the case were desperate, the prophet representing them as already in captivity though they had no reason to despair. Ellicott states the structural purpose, that the circumstances of misery which must intervene are placed side by side with the vision of returned glory, the king and the counsellors being powerless in the moment of emergency. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same turn as a shift of the prophet's eye from the glorious future to the immediate one, the loss of the royal government and the deportation. Calvin explains why contrary things are blended: the design is not to overturn what was promised but to support minds that might faint amid so many changes, so that the sense is that grievous troubles will arise capable of shaking the stoutest hearts, and yet God will redeem his people. Henry states the practical conclusion, that believers should cry aloud under distresses, but with the prayer of faith and not with despondency.

The naming of Babylon draws the sharpest historical comment. Ellicott observes that this prediction has naturally caused difficulty to those who doubt the power of prophets to prophesy, since Babylon was not considered at all in this prophet's day, when the other empire was in the ascendant, and it was a century afterwards before Babylon recovered its ancient dignity; and he lets the two facts stand together, that the prophet wrote the name and that the people of Judah did go there. Clarke reads the promise that follows as the whole arc, that there God would meet them, redeem them from captivity, bring them back to their own land and finally convert them to himself. Wesley fills in the intervening detail, the wars and the captivity, the lodging in open fields on the journey, the deliverance by three named kings as a type of a greater one, and a philological point the others miss, that the word rendered redeem denotes redemption by the next kinsman and so points to the Messiah.

The repeated word there is noticed by two voices as deliberate. Ellicott calls the repetition emphatic and matches it to the event, that the prophet had said the deliverance would happen in that place and that it did. Calvin explains why the emphasis was needed: the faithful might have shut out every hope of deliverance, as though the gate of God's power had been closed once they were carried off, and so the adverb is repeated to say that even from the grave he will deliver and redeem them. He is careful, though, not to let the promise soften the prospect. His reading of the opening imperatives is that the prophet gives leave to grieve, since even the strongest cannot look on such calamities without the heaviest sorrow; and the import of the whole is that although God would have a care for his people as he had promised, the faithful had no cause to flatter themselves that they would be exempt from troubles, but were rather exhorted to prepare to undergo them, being not only ejected from their country to wander like vagrants but led away as to their grave.
11:
Which gathering of nations is meant produces the chapter's most explicit clash. Clarke names the Chaldeans, themselves composed of many nations, with all the surrounding peoples who rejoiced when the city was overthrown. Gill considers that identification and rules it out, since those invaders succeeded and were conquerors rather than conquered, whereas the passage has them threshed; for the same reason he rejects the earlier Assyrian siege, that army having been destroyed by an angel and not by the daughter of Zion. His own preference is the times of the Maccabees; he reports that the Jewish commentators refer it to the armies of Gog and Magog in the days of a Messiah they still expect, that some Christian interpreters more probably understand the first times of the gospel, and that it may perhaps have its full accomplishment at the last battle. On the besiegers' cry they agree: Clarke has them wishing the city laid as low as it can be, like a thing defiled and cast away; Wesley has them asking that she be polluted with blood so that they may sack the temple; Ellicott glosses the looking as contemplating her destruction with pleasure, and points to the psalm recording the same calamity, the dwelling-place of the Name cast to the ground.

The reversal in the next verse is stated by everyone and pressed hardest by Gill and Clarke. Clarke gives the enemies' calculation, that they suppose God has utterly rejected his people and that they will be troubled by such a neighbour no more, whereas the affliction is for a time only and it is they who are gathered as sheaves to be trodden; and he names the neighbouring peoples afterwards subdued. Gill draws the general rule instead, that men know their own designs but not the Lord's, intending the ruin of others while God intends theirs, with the difference that his intentions are never frustrated and theirs are. Ellicott finds the closest parallel in the message about the haughty thoughts of the Assyrian king, who was told he had been no more than an instrument. Keil and Delitzsch give the two verses plainly without comment.

The threshing itself is where the readings divide again, and on a point of grammar. Clarke explains the iron horns and brazen hoofs as power and unconquerable strength, so that the enemies are no more against her than corn against oxen shod with brass, or a puny animal against the horn of a bull. Calvin agrees on the sense of the horn, which he says can mean elevation or dignity or power but here evidently means strength, and cites a Jewish paraphrase rendering it strong as iron and robust as brass. He then makes the opening imperative the point: the command to arise is emphatic because the church had been cast down so as to lie prostrate like a dead body without feeling, and God rouses her as by his voice alone, since raising the dead is his peculiar office, from which Calvin concludes that there is no reason for the faithful to despair when they find no strength or vigour left in them. Ellicott follows the same metaphor of oxen treading out corn, and then raises the textual question the others pass over: the better reading, supported by the old versions, puts the last promise in the second person, so that Zion herself is told she shall consecrate the spoil, rather than God saying that he will. Wesley reads the clause a third way, taking the first person for the church speaking of the spoils of her conquered enemies. Clarke keeps it as God's own act and asks whether it was not fulfilled when the sacred vessels were restored, adding that the Maccabees recovered much of the booty and devoted it; he also remarks that the first verse of the next chapter should have been made the conclusion of this one.
